subtopic: II.A clean and disinfect treatment areas
stem: In the correct order for treating an environmental surface, which step comes first?
choices: Applying the disinfectant and leaving it for the full contact time
Placing a new surface barrier over the area
Cleaning the surface to remove soil and microorganisms
Drying the surface with a clean paper towel
explanation: Cleaning physically removes large numbers of microorganisms and the debris that interferes with disinfectants, so it always comes before disinfection. Applying disinfectant first is the tempting choice, but disinfectant on a soiled surface may not work.
source_citation: CDC, Summary of Infection Prevention Practices in Dental Settings (2016), section: Environmental Infection Prevention and Control
source_quote: Cleaning removes large numbers of microorganisms from surfaces and should always precede disinfection.

stem: At the end of the day, an assistant is asked to clean the reception room floor, which has routine dust and dirt and no blood or body fluid contamination. What is appropriate?
choices: Detergent and water, or an EPA-registered hospital disinfectant/detergent
An FDA-cleared high-level disinfectant applied for its full immersion time
An intermediate-level disinfectant, because all office surfaces are clinical contact surfaces
No cleaning, because floors carry no risk and are cleaned only after spills
explanation: Housekeeping surfaces such as floors carry limited risk, and most need only detergent and water or a hospital disinfectant/detergent, depending on the surface and soil. An intermediate-level disinfectant is not needed for routine dust on a floor, and floors still need regular cleaning.
source_citation: CDC, Guidelines for Infection Control in Dental Health-Care Settings (2003), section: Environmental Infection Control, Housekeeping Surfaces
source_quote: The majority of housekeeping surfaces need to be cleaned only with a detergent and water or an EPA-registered hospital disinfectant/detergent, depending on the nature of the surface and the type and degree of contamination.

stem: In the in-office dental laboratory, how often should pressure pots and water baths be cleaned and disinfected?
choices: Once a week, as part of routine lab maintenance
Only when they are visibly soiled with stone or debris
At the end of each workday
Between patients
explanation: Pressure pots and water baths are especially prone to microbial contamination, so they are cleaned and disinfected between patients. Waiting until the end of the day lets contamination carry from one patient's case to the next.
source_citation: CDC, Guidelines for Infection Control in Dental Health-Care Settings (2003), section: Special Considerations, Dental Laboratory
source_quote: Pressure pots and water baths are particularly susceptible to contamination with microorganisms and should be cleaned and disinfected between patients

stem: After a patient leaves, the assistant sees blood spatter on the bracket tray, which was not covered by a barrier. After cleaning the tray, which disinfectant should be used?
choices: A low-level EPA-registered hospital disinfectant with an HIV and HBV claim
An EPA-registered hospital disinfectant with a tuberculocidal claim
A liquid chemical sterilant cleared by the FDA
A household cleaner followed by an alcohol wipe
explanation: Clinical contact surfaces that are visibly contaminated with blood call for an intermediate-level disinfectant, meaning one with a tuberculocidal claim. A low-level HIV/HBV product is fine for routine turnover but is not the recommendation when blood is visible.
source_citation: CDC, Summary of Infection Prevention Practices in Dental Settings (2016), section: Key Recommendations for Environmental Infection Prevention and Control in Dental Settings
source_quote: Clean and disinfect clinical contact surfaces that are not barrier-protected with an EPA-registered hospital disinfectant after each patient. Use an intermediate-level disinfectant (i.e., tuberculocidal claim) if visibly contaminated with blood.

stem: An EPA-registered hospital disinfectant is classified as intermediate-level when its label carries which additional claim?
choices: Sporicidal
Effective against HIV and HBV
FDA-cleared as a sterilant
Tuberculocidal
explanation: An intermediate-level disinfectant is an EPA-registered hospital disinfectant with a tuberculocidal label claim. An HIV and HBV claim is what OSHA requires of a low-level hospital disinfectant used on clinical contact surfaces, so it does not make a product intermediate-level.
source_citation: CDC, Guidelines for Infection Control in Dental Health-Care Settings (2003), section: Selected Definitions
source_quote: Intermediate-level disinfectant: Liquid chemical germicide registered with EPA as a hospital disinfectant and with a label claim of potency as tuberculocidal

stem: An assistant wants to use a single spray product to both preclean and then disinfect a countertop during room turnover. When is using the disinfectant as the cleaner acceptable?
choices: When the product label states it is suitable for use as a cleaner
Whenever the product is an EPA-registered hospital disinfectant
Only when the countertop has no visible soil
Whenever the product has a tuberculocidal claim
explanation: A disinfectant should not be used as a cleaner unless its label says it is suitable for that use, as with a detergent/disinfectant. EPA registration or a tuberculocidal claim describes germ-killing ability, not cleaning ability, so neither alone makes the product a cleaner.
source_citation: CDC, Summary of Infection Prevention Practices in Dental Settings (2016), section: Environmental Infection Prevention and Control
source_quote: Disinfectant products should not be used as cleaners unless the label indicates the product is suitable for such use.

subtopic: II.C surface barriers, surface check after removal
stem: Still gloved, an assistant removes the plastic barrier from the chair switch after a patient. The switch underneath looks clean and dry. What does CDC guidance say about disinfecting the switch?
choices: Always disinfect it with an intermediate-level disinfectant before a new barrier
Disinfect it with a low-level disinfectant, since it was covered during treatment
Clean and disinfect it only if contamination is evident
Disinfect it only at the end of the day, since a barrier was used
explanation: After removing a barrier, examine the surface; it needs cleaning and disinfection only if contamination is evident. Routinely disinfecting under an intact barrier is tempting but is not required, since preventing that step is the purpose of the barrier.
source_citation: CDC, Guidelines for Infection Control in Dental Health-Care Settings (2003), section: Environmental Infection Control, Clinical Contact Surfaces
source_quote: After removing the barrier, examine the surface to make sure it did not become soiled inadvertently. The surface needs to be cleaned and disinfected only if contamination is evident.

subtopic: II.C surface barriers, placing new barriers
stem: An assistant has removed all contaminated barriers from the operatory with gloved hands, and every surface looks clean. What should happen before the fresh barriers go on?
choices: Put a second pair of gloves over the contaminated ones
Remove the gloves and perform hand hygiene
Spray the gloved hands with surface disinfectant
Place the new barriers immediately with the same gloves
explanation: Clean barriers are placed after removing the contaminated gloves and performing hand hygiene, so the new covers are not contaminated as they go on. Keeping the same gloves on would transfer contamination straight to the clean barriers.
source_citation: CDC, Guidelines for Infection Control in Dental Health-Care Settings (2003), section: Environmental Infection Control, Clinical Contact Surfaces
source_quote: Otherwise, after removing gloves and performing hand hygiene, DHCP should place clean barriers on these surfaces before the next patient

stem: Which of these items is an example of a single-use (disposable) device in dentistry?
choices: Plastic orthodontic bracket
Metal impression tray
Mouth mirror
Face bow fork
explanation: CDC lists plastic orthodontic brackets, along with needles and prophy cups and brushes, as single-use devices that are usually not heat-tolerant and cannot be reliably cleaned. Metal impression trays and face bow forks are heat-tolerant and are heat-sterilized between patients.
source_citation: CDC, Guidelines for Infection Control in Dental Health-Care Settings (2003), section: Special Considerations, Single-Use or Disposable Devices
source_quote: Single-use devices in dentistry are usually not heat-tolerant and cannot be reliably cleaned. Examples include syringe needles, prophylaxis cups and brushes, and plastic orthodontic brackets.

stem: About half of a single-dose vial of medication is left after one patient's procedure. The next patient needs the same medication. What should the assistant do with the leftover?
choices: Use it for the next patient if a new sterile needle and syringe are used
Save it by combining it with other leftover vials of the same drug
Wipe the stopper with alcohol and store it for later that day
Discard it and open a new vial for the next patient
explanation: Single-dose vials are never used for more than one patient, and leftovers are not combined for later use. Using a new needle and syringe is the tempting answer, but it does not make a single-dose vial safe for a second patient.
source_citation: CDC, Summary of Infection Prevention Practices in Dental Settings (2016), section: Key Recommendations for Safe Injection Practices
source_quote: Do not use single-dose (single-use) medication vials, ampules, and bags or bottles of intravenous solution for more than one patient.

subtopic: II.D tray setup, sterile package integrity
stem: While pulling a wrapped instrument cassette from the cabinet to set up a tray, the assistant finds a tear in the wrap. What should be done with the instruments?
choices: Use them if the internal chemical indicator changed color
Tape the tear closed and use the cassette for the next patient
Reclean them, package them in new wrap, and sterilize them again
Wipe them with an intermediate-level disinfectant before use
explanation: Once packaging is compromised, the contents can no longer be considered sterile, so the instruments are recleaned, rewrapped, and resterilized. Taping the tear closed does not restore sterility, and neither does a chemical indicator that changed color during the original cycle.
source_citation: CDC, Guidelines for Infection Control in Dental Health-Care Settings (2003), section: Storage of Sterilized Items and Clean Dental Supplies
source_quote: If packaging is compromised, the instruments should be recleaned, packaged in new wrap, and sterilized again.

subtopic: II.E dental unit waterlines, water quality standard
stem: At a minimum, water used as coolant or irrigant for nonsurgical dental procedures should contain how many heterotrophic bacteria?
choices: Fewer than 5,000 CFU/mL
Fewer than 500 CFU/mL
Fewer than 200,000 CFU/mL
Zero CFU/mL, meaning sterile water
explanation: Nonsurgical treatment water should meet the EPA drinking water standard of fewer than 500 CFU/mL at a minimum. Sterile water is required only for surgical procedures, not routine care.
source_citation: CDC, Guidelines for Infection Control in Dental Health-Care Settings (2003), section: Dental Unit Waterlines, Biofilm, and Water Quality
source_quote: the number of bacteria in water used as a coolant/irrigant for nonsurgical dental procedures should be as low as reasonably achievable and, at a minimum, <500 CFU/mL, the regulatory standard for safe drinking water established by EPA and APHA/AWWA.

subtopic: II.E dental unit waterlines, flushing between patients
stem: The dental unit has antiretraction valves. Between patients, what should be done with the high-speed handpiece and the air/water syringe?
choices: Nothing, because antiretraction valves prevent oral fluids from entering the lines
Run water and air through them for about 5 seconds
Flush them for 2 minutes, but only at the start of each clinic day
Discharge water and air through them for at least 20 to 30 seconds
explanation: Any device connected to the dental water system that enters the mouth should discharge water and air for at least 20 to 30 seconds after each patient to flush out patient material. CDC recommends this even when antiretraction valves are present.
source_citation: CDC, Guidelines for Infection Control in Dental Health-Care Settings (2003), section: Recommendations, VIII. Dental Unit Waterlines, Biofilm, and Water Quality
source_quote: Discharge water and air for a minimum of 20--30 seconds after each patient, from any device connected to the dental water system that enters the patient's mouth

subtopic: II.E dental unit waterlines, biofilm control
stem: An office fills its self-contained water bottles with distilled water and flushes the lines each morning, but uses no waterline treatment product. Why is this unlikely to keep treatment water within standards?
choices: Biofilm in the lines is not controlled, and removing it requires chemical germicides
Distilled water contains more bacteria than tap water
Morning flushing must last at least 30 minutes to be effective
Self-contained bottles cannot be used with distilled water
explanation: Clean source water will not keep treatment water clean if biofilm in the waterlines is not controlled, and removing or inactivating biofilm requires chemical germicides. Longer flushing is tempting, but flushing does not affect biofilm.
source_citation: CDC, Guidelines for Infection Control in Dental Health-Care Settings (2003), section: Strategies To Improve Dental Unit Water Quality
source_quote: Simply using source water containing <500 CFU/mL of bacteria (e.g., tap, distilled, or sterile water) in a self-contained water system will not eliminate bacterial contamination in treatment water if biofilms in the water system are not controlled. Removal or inactivation of dental waterline biofilms requires use of chemical germicides.

subtopic: II.E dental unit waterlines, surgical irrigation
stem: The dentist is about to perform a surgical extraction that requires a flap. How should the coolant/irrigant be delivered?
choices: Fill the unit's independent reservoir with sterile water and use the handpiece as usual
Use treated dental unit water that has tested below 500 CFU/mL
Deliver sterile saline or sterile water with a device such as a sterile bulb syringe
Use tap water that has been boiled and cooled in the reservoir bottle
explanation: Surgical procedures need sterile solutions delivered through a sterile device, such as a bulb syringe or sterile single-use tubing. Filling the reservoir with sterile water is the tempting choice, but the unit's water pathway cannot be reliably sterilized, so the water will not stay sterile.
source_citation: CDC, Guidelines for Infection Control in Dental Health-Care Settings (2003), section: Delivery of Sterile Surgical Irrigation
source_quote: Conventional dental units cannot reliably deliver sterile water even when equipped with independent water reservoirs because the water-bearing pathway cannot be reliably sterilized. Delivery devices (e.g., bulb syringe or sterile, single-use disposable products) should be used to deliver sterile water

stem: During a bonding appointment, a patient asks whether they should close their lips tightly around the saliva ejector to help it work. What should the assistant tell them?
choices: Yes, a tight seal improves suction and keeps the field dry
No, a tight seal can pull fluid from the suction line back into the mouth
Yes, but only when the high-volume evacuator is also running
No, because it will clog the saliva ejector tip with debris
explanation: Closing the lips around the saliva ejector can create a partial vacuum that lets fluid and microorganisms in the line flow back into the patient's mouth, so patients should not be told to do it. Running the high-volume evacuator at the same time makes backflow more likely, not less.
source_citation: CDC, Guidelines for Infection Control in Dental Health-Care Settings (2003), section: Recommendations, IX.A Dental Handpieces and Other Devices Attached to Air and Waterlines
source_quote: Do not advise patients to close their lips tightly around the tip of the saliva ejector to evacuate oral fluids

subtopic: II.F evacuation, tubing position and backflow
stem: Which setup makes it more likely that fluid in the low-volume suction line will flow back toward the patient's mouth?
choices: The saliva ejector tubing is draped so a length of it sits above the patient's mouth
The saliva ejector tubing hangs below the level of the patient's mouth
A new disposable saliva ejector tip is placed for each patient
The high-volume evacuator is turned off while the saliva ejector runs
explanation: Gravity pulls fluid back toward the patient whenever part of the suction tubing holding the tip is positioned above the mouth. Turning the high-volume evacuator off is not the risk; using it at the same time as the saliva ejector is what promotes backflow.
source_citation: CDC, Guidelines for Infection Control in Dental Health-Care Settings (2003), section: Special Considerations, Saliva Ejectors
source_quote: gravity pulls fluid back toward the patient's mouth whenever a length of the suction tubing holding the tip is positioned above the patient's mouth, or during simultaneous use of other evacuation (high-volume) equipment

stem: How should the radiograph tubehead and control panel be protected during patient care?
choices: Wiped with disinfectant once at the end of the day
Covered with barriers that are changed at the end of the day
Cleaned only if they become visibly soiled with blood
Covered with surface barriers that are changed after each patient
explanation: Radiography equipment such as the tubehead and control panel should have surface barriers changed after each patient. Changing barriers only at the end of the day would let contamination from gloved hands pass between patients.
source_citation: CDC, Guidelines for Infection Control in Dental Health-Care Settings (2003), section: Special Considerations, Dental Radiology
source_quote: Radiography equipment (e.g., radiograph tubehead and control panel) should be protected with surface barriers that are changed after each patient.

stem: A digital sensor cannot tolerate heat sterilization or high-level disinfection. It was covered with an FDA-cleared barrier, and the barrier looked intact when removed. What should be done before the next patient?
choices: Nothing, because the intact barrier kept the sensor clean
Clean the sensor and disinfect it with an intermediate-level EPA-registered hospital disinfectant
Wipe the sensor with a low-level disinfectant only if saliva is visible
Place a second barrier over the sensor without cleaning it
explanation: Barriers on sensors can fail without looking torn, so after the barrier is removed the sensor is cleaned and disinfected with an intermediate-level hospital disinfectant after each patient. Relying on a barrier that looks intact is the tempting mistake.
source_citation: CDC, Guidelines for Infection Control in Dental Health-Care Settings (2003), section: Special Considerations, Dental Radiology
source_quote: To minimize the potential for device-associated infections, after removing the barrier, the device should be cleaned and disinfected with an EPA-registered hospital disinfectant (intermediate-level) after each patient.

subtopic: II.H disinfect impressions before sending to the lab
stem: An assistant takes an alginate impression for a retainer that will go to an off-site lab. What should be done before it is packaged?
choices: Rinse it under water and bag it, since the lab will disinfect it on arrival
Spray it with any surface disinfectant and seal it in the bag while still wet
Clean it, disinfect it with a tuberculocidal EPA-registered hospital disinfectant, and rinse it
Let it dry on the counter so the disinfectant will adhere better later
explanation: Impressions are cleaned, disinfected with a tuberculocidal hospital disinfectant, and rinsed before they are handled in the office lab or sent out. Leaving disinfection to the lab is tempting but exposes everyone who handles the case in transit.
source_citation: CDC, Guidelines for Infection Control in Dental Health-Care Settings (2003), section: Special Considerations, Dental Laboratory
source_quote: should be thoroughly cleaned (i.e., blood and bioburden removed), disinfected with an EPA-registered hospital disinfectant with a tuberculocidal claim, and thoroughly rinsed before being handled in the in-office laboratory or sent to an off-site laboratory

stem: When is the best time to clean and disinfect an impression or appliance?
choices: As soon as possible after it is removed from the patient's mouth
After the stone model has been poured
At the end of the day, along with the other lab cases
After the lab confirms it has received the case
explanation: Cleaning and disinfecting right after removal from the mouth keeps blood and other bioburden from drying on the item. Waiting until after the model is poured is tempting but lets microorganisms move onto the cast.
source_citation: CDC, Guidelines for Infection Control in Dental Health-Care Settings (2003), section: Special Considerations, Dental Laboratory
source_quote: The best time to clean and disinfect impressions, prostheses, or appliances is as soon as possible after removal from the patient's mouth before drying of blood or other bioburden can occur.

subtopic: II.H final disinfection of returned appliances
stem: A retainer comes back from the dental laboratory in a sealed bag, with no written note about whether or how it was disinfected. Who is responsible for final disinfection before delivery?
choices: The laboratory, so the case should be sent back to them
No one, because appliances from a lab arrive clean
The patient, who should soak it at home before wearing it
The dental office, before the retainer is delivered
explanation: If the lab does not provide written documentation of its disinfection method, the dental office is responsible for final disinfection. Assuming the sealed bag means the lab disinfected it is the tempting error.
source_citation: CDC, Guidelines for Infection Control in Dental Health-Care Settings (2003), section: Special Considerations, Dental Laboratory
source_quote: If such documentation is not provided, the dental office is responsible for final disinfection procedures.

stem: Which of these items should be handled as regulated medical waste rather than general office waste?
choices: Exam gloves used during a routine wire change
Gauze saturated with blood after a surgical extraction
A plastic barrier removed from the light handle
Cotton rolls lightly soiled with saliva
explanation: Solid waste soaked or saturated with blood or saliva, such as gauze after surgery, is regulated waste. Used gloves, environmental barriers, and lightly soiled cotton rolls are general medical waste that can go with ordinary trash.
source_citation: CDC, Guidelines for Infection Control in Dental Health-Care Settings (2003), section: Nonregulated and Regulated Medical Waste
source_quote: Examples of regulated waste found in dental-practice settings are solid waste soaked or saturated with blood or saliva (e.g., gauze saturated with blood after surgery), extracted teeth, surgically removed hard and soft tissues, and contaminated sharp items (e.g., needles, scalpel blades, and wires)

stem: After an archwire is placed, the assistant clips the distal ends. Where do the cut wire pieces go?
choices: The general trash, since the pieces are too small to cause injury
A biohazard bag along with blood-saturated gauze
A puncture-resistant sharps container
The instrument cassette, to be sterilized and discarded later
explanation: Orthodontic wires are sharp items and belong in a puncture-resistant container. A biohazard bag is tempting because it is regulated waste, but a bag can be punctured by wire ends.
source_citation: CDC, Guidelines for Infection Control in Dental Health-Care Settings (2003), section: Special Considerations, Dental Laboratory
source_quote: Personnel should dispose of sharp items (e.g., burs, disposable blades, and orthodontic wires) in puncture-resistant containers.
